Establishing credible fiscal institutions and fiscal buffers. When a shock hits,
the fiscal impact can be immediate and large, as spending needed to protect
vulnerable communities rises while revenues fall. Governments can prepare
for this tendency by establishing contingency reserves within the annual
budget, natural disaster funds with clear rules governing their use and size
calibrated to historical experience, and state-contingent debt instruments
and other insurance mechanisms that transfer a portion of disaster risk to
third parties (Polacek 2018). Well-designed fiscal rules can reinforce these
buffers while allowing temporary, transparent flexibility during severe shocks.
These instruments should be integrated into broader fiscal risk and debt-
management frameworks. Contingent liabilities, including guarantees to state-
owned enterprises, public-private partnerships, financial sector support, and
disaster-related obligations, should be identified, monitored, and disclosed.
Medium-term expenditure frameworks offer one powerful mechanism for
translating these commitments into practice, aligning spending with strategic
priorities and ensuring the planning horizon needed to address future shocks
before they arrive (World Bank 2012).
Food Import Exposure, External Debt Burdens, and
Healthy Diet Affordability
Food imports are an important channel through which external shocks can
affect food and nutrition security. They are particularly relevant as countries face
an uncertain external environment, with geopolitical tensions, weather-related
shocks, trade disruptions, and volatility in energy and fertilizer markets posing
continued risks to global food markets and prices (FAO 2026; World Bank
2026a). Such shocks may be especially difficult to absorb in economies with high
external debt burdens. In countries that rely more heavily on imported food, such
shocks can translate into higher domestic food prices, with potentially important
implications for household purchasing power, welfare, and diet quality, given the
substantial share of food in household consumption, especially in lower-income
countries (FAO and World Bank 2018).
Previous analysis in International Debt Report 2025 showed that higher external
debt burdens were associated with higher levels of unaffordability of healthy
diets across countries (World Bank 2025). This section extends that analysis
by examining food import exposure as one important source of vulnerability
to external shocks, including the importance of food in merchandise imports,
reliance on imported supply across food groups, and the diversification of import
sources. It also examines associations between external debt burdens and changes
71

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
in healthy diet unaffordability over time, a broader outcome that reflects both
food costs and people’s economic resources.
Food Import Shares in Poorer Economies
Across the sample, which consists predominantly of LMICs, the share of food in
merchandise imports generally declines as income per capita rises (figure 2.13,
panel a). By contrast, economies with larger external debt burdens relative to
exports also tend to have higher food import shares (figure 2.13, panel b).5
Both relationships matter for an economy’s capacity to manage food import
exposure. Lower-income economies may have less room to absorb increases in
import costs, and a high debt-to-exports ratio indicates that external debt is
large relative to export earnings. During external shocks, higher import costs can
therefore coincide with weaker economic and external buffers; export earnings
may also decline, further increasing pressure on foreign exchange resources and
raising the debt-to-exports ratio, even without an increase in the debt stock.
Import Reliance and Debt Burdens Across Food Groups
Aggregate food import shares do not show how strongly the domestic supply of
individual food groups depends on international markets. Net import reliance—
net imports as a share of domestic supply quantity—varies substantially across
the six food groups making up the Healthy Diet Basket (Bai, Herforth et al. 2025;
Herforth et al. 2025). Among net importing economies, median reliance is highest
for oils and fats, at 63.6 percent, followed by starchy staples, at 36.9 percent, and
legumes, nuts, and seeds, at 34.1 percent. Median reliance is lower for animal-
source foods, at 28.0 percent, and for vegetables and fruits, at 17.4 percent and
13.4 percent, respectively.
To identify economies where high reliance on food imports and elevated
external debt burdens overlap, figure 2.13 applies two reference thresholds. For
many economies, high import reliance coincides with elevated external debt
burdens. Figure 2.14 highlights economies where external debt stocks are at
least 150 percent of exports, as a reference point based on the threshold applied
under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative,6 and where net
imports account for at least 30 percent of domestic supply in a given food
group. The figure intends to identify the coexistence of these two sources of
vulnerability, rather than to assess whether higher external debt is associated
with greater reliance on food imports. This overlap is most common for oils and
fats: 34 economies—about 42 percent of net importers in the group—meet both
thresholds. The corresponding shares are about 28 percent for legumes, nuts,
and seeds; 27 percent for starchy staples; 23 percent for animal-source foods;
16 percent for vegetables; and 15 percent for fruits.

Diversifying Import Sources to Improve Resilience
Import reliance, however, captures only one dimension of exposure. Another is
how concentrated imports are across source economies. An economy that sources
a food group from a broader range of suppliers may have more options to adjust
when trade with a particular exporter is disrupted than one that depends on only
a few sources. Import source diversity is measured using the Shannon Diversity
Index,7 which captures both the number of source economies and how evenly
imports are distributed across them; higher values indicate greater diversification.
Higher-income economies generally source food imports from a broader and more
evenly distributed set of suppliers (Bai, Kaushik et al. 2025). In the sample used for
this analysis, upper-middle-income economies have higher median import source
diversity than low- and lower-middle-income economies in five of the six food groups,

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs
Among economies covered by this analysis, healthy diet unaffordability remains
particularly high in LICs. The population-weighted prevalence of people unable
to afford a healthy diet fell only marginally, from 77.4 percent in 2017 to
76.9 percent in 2025, and increased by 4.0 percentage points during 2019–21.
Between 2017 and 2025, unaffordability declined from 58.5 to 45.2 percent in
lower-middle-income economies and from 34.2 to 23.2 percent in upper-middle-
income economies.
During 2017–19, the relationship between changes in healthy diet unaffordability
and external debt burdens was weak and not statistically significant. The
association became substantially stronger and statistically significant during
2019–21 and remained similarly strong and significant during 2021–23. In these
periods, economies with higher debt stocks relative to export earnings tended to
experience larger increases, or smaller declines, in healthy diet unaffordability.
A doubling of the debt-to-exports ratio was associated with a more adverse change
in unaffordability of approximately 1.6–1.8 percentage points. During 2023–25,
the relationship weakened again and was no longer statistically significant.
As revealed in this section, food import vulnerability reflects both reliance on
imported supply and the concentration of import sources, and these dimensions
can coincide with high external debt burdens. The period analysis adds an
outcome perspective, showing that higher debt burdens are more strongly
associated with nutrition security challenges during major external shocks, as
reflected in changes in healthy diet unaffordability. This pattern is consistent with
the earlier framing of debt acting as an amplifier of vulnerability, and it highlights
the importance of considering food import exposure and external debt together
when assessing a country’s nutrition resilience to future external shocks.

3. Advancing Debt Transparency
Introduction
Over the past five years, the debt transparency agenda has moved decisively from
an aspiration to a reality, translating commitments into tangible improvements in
the coverage, accuracy, timeliness, and usability of debt data. This progress comes
at a critical moment. As the prior chapters of this report show, the external debt
stock of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and the costs of servicing
that debt are at a record high, putting increasing pressure on public finances in
many LMICs and crowding out critical social and development spending. In this
environment, strengthening debt transparency is not merely a statistical objective;
instead, it is an essential foundation for sound fiscal management, effective risk
assessment, informed policy making, and financial stability.
This chapter charts the progress made to date to enhance debt transparency in
LMICs and discusses the important initiatives currently under way to scale up the
debt transparency agenda.
Progress in Debt Transparency, 2020–25
Debt transparency is at the center of the World Bank Group’s engagement
with its borrowers and partners. The policy commitment of the International
Development Association (IDA) is to support debt sustainability and debt
transparency through technical assistance, knowledge, and financing
engagements. The Sustainable Development Finance Policy (SDFP), which
became effective in July 2020, requires IDA-eligible borrowers at moderate or
elevated risk of debt distress to take concrete policy performance actions (PPAs)
to enhance debt transparency, strengthen debt management, and promote fiscal
sustainability.1 These PPAs have been instrumental in incentivizing countries to
embrace sustainable development financing, embed debt transparency reforms
into national policy frameworks, and institutionalize transparent disclosure of
public debt data. The policy also leverages IDA’s global convening capacity to
foster closer coordination among creditors to mitigate debt-related vulnerabilities,
which has facilitated the reconciliation of data reported by borrowers to the
World Bank Group Debtor Reporting System (DRS) with data made available by
bilateral creditors. Consequently, asymmetries between the two data sets have

Since the SDFP policy became effective, a total of 887 PPAs have been agreed,
of which 60 percent focused on debt transparency and debt management and 40
percent on fiscal sustainability. In its first year in operation, fiscal year (FY) 2021,
55 IDA countries committed to 130 PPAs. By FY2026, these numbers had risen to
65 IDA countries implementing 159 PPAs, of which 55 percent focused on debt
transparency and debt management. During the initial years of implementation,
PPAs related to debt transparency focused on foundational measures aimed at
disclosure of timely and comprehensive debt bulletins. More recently, the focus
has shifted to monitoring and disclosure of contingent liabilities, borrowing by
state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and actions that institutionalize timely debt
monitoring and reporting. Overall, PPAs related to debt transparency have fallen
from 32 percent of total PPAs in FY2021 to 10 percent in FY2026, reflecting
progress made in disclosure of debt data. However, the sustained implementation
of reform measures in some IDA countries has proved challenging, particularly
in states categorized as fragile and conflict affected. In addition, with tighter
global financing conditions, some governments have turned to off-budget and
increasingly complex debt instruments—including bilateral currency swaps, total
return swaps, and collateralized loans—to meet financing needs, making it harder
to assess public debt exposure.
The SDFP has consistently prioritized debt management, and the share of PPAs
in debt management has remained steady, rising from 41 percent of total PPAs
in FY2021 to 45 percent in FY2026. Debt management PPAs address risks
stemming from high debt levels by ensuring compliance with nonconcessional
borrowing ceilings. They also focus on strengthening institutional structures
for debt management, including the creation of dedicated debt offices, strong
legal and governance frameworks, and enhanced procedures for managing
sovereign guarantees, on-lending, and borrowing by SOEs. Future PPAs in debt
management will continue to address gaps in legislative frameworks, institutional
fragmentation, and inadequate oversight of public borrowing. The SDFP also
plays a catalytic role in advancing reforms related to the management of domestic
debt and the development of domestic debt markets. These reforms have included
PPAs that supported the formulation and publication of medium-term debt
strategies with clear targets for domestic and external borrowing in Fiji, the
Kyrgyz Republic, Nigeria, the Solomon Islands, and Sri Lanka, and publication of
annual borrowing plans that include domestic borrowing in the Central African
Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, and St. Lucia. PPAs have also supported the development
of operational guidelines for the issuance of government bonds in the domestic
market in Bangladesh, the Solomon Islands, and Tonga; the strengthening of

The World Bank Group tracks progress in borrowing countries’ public debt
dissemination practices on an annual basis. Its assessment of these outcomes
is presented in a heat map that measures the strengths and weaknesses of the
dissemination practices in 76 IDA-eligible countries across nine key indicators:
data accessibility, instrument coverage, sectoral coverage, information on recently
contracted external loans, periodicity, time lag, debt management strategy, annual
borrowing plan, and additional statistics and memo items.2
The Debt Reporting Heat Map shows that, over the past five years, IDA-eligible
borrowers have made significant progress in public debt disclosure practices.
In 2020, only 36 IDA-eligible countries, 47 percent of the 76 countries covered
by the heat map, published fully accessible public debt data. The 2025 heat
map found that 54 countries, or 72 percent, had fully accessible public debt
data, a 25-percentage-point gain from 2020 (figure 3.1). Data accessibility in
Sub-Saharan African countries has also improved significantly, rising from
19 countries (50 percent of countries in the region) that published fully accessible
data in 2020, to 29 countries (or 76 percent) in 2025 despite a regression
in accessibility of data in some countries. These countries include Ethiopia,
where data accessibility had deteriorated since it defaulted on its international
bond in 2023, and Senegal, following the revelation by the auditors of a large
understatement in the official debt statistics. Even in countries that have accessible
data, important information gaps persist. Instrument coverage has improved,
with 45 countries assessed as having full coverage in 2025 compared to 33
countries in 2020, but progress has been slower than accessibility. Additionally,
comprehensive sector coverage is limited, with subnational borrowing, contingent
liabilities, and the obligations of SOE debt often excluded from the official public
debt figure. Moreover, only about one-quarter of countries report instrument-

Significant progress has been made to improve the quality, coverage, and
consistency of external debt statistics through systematic debtor-creditor
reconciliation exercises. At the core of this initiative is the reconciliation of loan-
by-loan information on public and publicly guaranteed external debt reported by
borrowers to the DRS with corresponding data provided by bilateral creditors.
This process enables cross-checking of data sets, identification of discrepancies,
validation of loan terms and transactions, and filling of critical data gaps, all of
which serve to enhance the accuracy of debt statistics.
Initiated in 2022, these exercises have become a central element of the broader
debt transparency agenda, supporting more accurate debt monitoring, improved
data validation, and better-informed debt analysis in IDA-eligible countries.
The first reconciliation exercise, conducted using end-2021 data, covered 3,655
individual loans and loan tranches reported by 18 creditor countries, including
all Group of Seven (G-7) members and 11 Paris Club creditors. Approximately
80 percent of loans were successfully matched, representing about 90 percent
of total outstanding debt values, providing a first comprehensive assessment of
discrepancies between debtor and creditor records. Despite a remaining overall
difference of about 10 percent, the exercise provided critical insights into the
nature and sources of discrepancies and established a strong foundation for
future rounds.

The third and most recent round of the reconciliation exercise, using end-2024
data, demonstrated substantial progress in aligning the debtor and creditor data
sets for both scale and accuracy. Again, 18 creditors participated and together
reported 4,875 individual loans and loan tranches, representing $63.4 billion
in outstanding debt, out of which a total of 3,762 loans and loan tranches
(77 percent) were matched to their counterpart in the DRS database (figure 3.3).
For matched loans, creditor-reported claims of $58.0 billion differed by less than
1 percent from the comparable figure reported by debtors to the DRS, indicating
that remaining gaps are relatively limited in magnitude.
The overall reporting gap, equivalent to $5.4 billion, masks much wider variations
for individual creditors, but the reconciliation exercise found that gaps are also
progressively narrowing. Figure 3.4 compares the total end-2024 claims reported
by each of the 18 creditors with the total debt owed to each creditor that debtors
reported to the DRS. Points on the dashed line indicate perfect alignment between
debtor and creditor reporting. For 6 of the 18 participating creditors, the end-2024
claims align fully with the comparable figure reported by borrowers to the DRS,
and for 2 creditors the gap was small. For other creditors, where larger differences
were observed, these differences were typically concentrated in a small number
of loans and found to be primarily the result of misclassification or differences in
reporting norms, not true errors. As the chart also shows, discrepancies are not
one directional: points above the dashed line indicate that claims reported by the
creditor are higher than the comparable amount reported by the debtor, and points
below the line reflect cases where the debtor figure is higher than the creditor.
The reconciliation exercises have highlighted that asymmetries between debtor
and creditor data are not driven solely by gaps in debtor country reporting.
Rather, they arise from several factors including differences in definitions,
reporting practices, and institutional coordination. On the debtor side, these
factors include (a) weak debt management, which limits timely, comprehensive
recording of debt liabilities; (b) time lags in reporting new commitments and
disbursements; (c) understatement of arrears, particularly penalty interest
charges, often due to the complexity of how these are calculated; (d) failure
to report, which results in estimated data by World Bank Group staff; and
(e) misclassification of direct and guaranteed export credits. Creditor-side factors
include (a) lack of standard methodology and variation in national accounting
norms; (b) the practice of some creditors to record disbursements as loan tranches
without reference to the original loan commitment; (c) potential double-counting
of bilateral lending delivered through common funds such as the European
Economic Community–IDA trust fund and captured in the DRS as multilateral
debt; and (d) inclusion of claims that are not external public sector, such as loans
to private sector entities.

Other reasons for asymmetries between the debtor and creditor data include
recording of indemnification of payment arrears to private creditors on
guaranteed export credits typically captured in debtor data only when a formal

for recording forgiveness of bilateral claims and bilateral debt swaps that
extinguish external debt obligations in return for investment of the local currency
equivalent in a dedicated fund for specific expenditures such as education or
measures to mitigate climate change.
The reconciliation process has strengthened dialogue and underscored
mutual accountability and the need for standardized reporting frameworks.
Currently, DRS submissions provide more granular and complete
information—such as loan-level details, disbursements, and terms—which
are not always fully mirrored in creditor data sets. At the same time, the
reconciliation exercises have played a critical role in identifying persistent data
gaps, particularly regarding the liabilities of SOEs and structural weaknesses

Since the reconciliation process began, tangible progress has taken place in
creditor engagement. An increasing number of creditors provided a detailed
response to follow-up queries and provided data clarification, contributing to
more accurate gap-filling and reconciliation outcomes, reflecting a transition
toward systematic collaboration. Building on this momentum will be critical to
resolving remaining discrepancies and ensuring that the reconciliation exercise
continues to deliver sustained improvements in data quality, transparency,
and comparability. Overall, these data-sharing and reconciliation efforts have
already significantly narrowed asymmetries between borrower and creditor
data, strengthened the credibility of debt statistics, and improved the analytical
foundation for monitoring debt vulnerabilities. As discussed in the following
sections, continued collaboration, expanded participation, and ongoing
methodological enhancements are expected to further advance data quality,
transparency, and global comparability of debt statistics.
Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda
The DRS is a long-standing, cross-country comparable database on external
debt for LMICs. Initially established in 1951 for institutional purposes to
collect accurate and timely data on external public debt to evaluate borrowers’
90

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
foreign currency obligations and assess creditworthiness, it evolved into a global
public good, International Debt Statistics (IDS), which plays a central role in
promoting debt transparency through the provision of standardized, cross-
country comparable information on external debt levels in LMICs. Together,
the DRS and the IDS are the backbone of the World Bank Group’s debt
transparency architecture.
Building a New Generation of Debt Statistics
The DRS collects detailed, instrument-level information on public and
publicly guaranteed external debt from IBRD and IDA borrowers to support
the operational work of the World Bank Group. This work includes debt
sustainability analysis, country diagnostics, debt transparency assessments,
technical assistance, reform programs, and policy dialogue on macroeconomic
outcomes and goals. Through its long-standing engagement with national
debt offices, ministries of finance, and central banks, the DRS has become the
central platform for methodological alignment, data validation, and institutional
strengthening.
The IDS, the World Bank Group’s flagship statistical database on external
debt, underpins the annual publication of the International Debt Report and
serves as the primary global repository of external debt data for LMICs. It
draws on data reported to the DRS and complementary information from other
sources, including multilateral and bilateral creditors, international financial
institutions, market data, and other statistical data sets to create the world’s most
comprehensive and globally comparable statistical resource for policy makers,
investors, researchers, and development partners. (Refer to annex 3A for more
information on sources of debt statistics.) Complementary databases updated
quarterly—Quarterly External Debt Statistics and Quarterly Public Sector Debt—
provide high-frequency data that support the monitoring of evolving debt trends
for the current year.
Modernizing and Expanding the DRS
The DRS is currently undergoing the most extensive makeover since it was first
implemented in the 1950s. The rationale for this modernization and expansion
is threefold. The process aims to (a) introduce a new reporting framework and
more comprehensive instrument-level reporting that responds to the changes in
the global financial architecture and multiplicity of borrowing instruments now
available to LMICs; (b) bring DRS reporting norms into conformity with the most
recent international standards and definitions for recording and compiling debt
statistics; and (c) take advantage of the latest advances in technology, including
91

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
where appropriate artificial intelligence, to streamline and simplify the reporting
process, assist reporters with queries about reporting protocols, and validate the
consistency of data. The new DRS framework, which will be finalized and rolled
out in the coming year, represents a major step forward in strengthening the
global debt data architecture.
The reporting framework is being expanded to introduce more comprehensive
instrument-level reporting, including additional information on loan
characteristics, debtor and creditor guarantees, collateral arrangements, debt
reorganization, creditor attributes, and emerging financing instruments such
as total return swaps, third party discounted buybacks, and asset-backed
financing. The reporting requirements are designed to capture a comprehensive
and much richer picture of all the basic characteristics of each debt instrument,
such as borrower, lender, and associated terms. For example, additional
reporting fields require the reporter to provide information on the type of
debt security and the market and nominal value at the end of each reporting
period. This information facilitates a more comprehensive analysis, such as
an evaluation of the impact of market fluctuations on the valuation of debt
instruments and alignment and comparison with the international statistical
standards, in this case the liabilities recorded by the International Monetary
Fund (IMF) International Investment Position. The reporting standards and
definitions are aligned to the latest international statistical standards, including
the revised IMF directives on the compilation of balance of payments statistics
from the seventh edition of the IMF’s Integrated Balance of Payments and
International Investment Position Manual (IMF 2025) and the United Nations
Statistics Division’s 2025 System of National Accounts.
The new state-of-the-art DRS platform represents a radical change from
the prior mechanism for the collection and compilation of debt data. It is
structured around three key modules: data collection, data management, and
reporting and analytics that take full advantage of the latest technological
developments. The platform is designed to meet several key objectives: simplify
and improve reporting efficiency for borrowers; incorporate automated data
validation processes; enhance analytical capabilities; and facilitate greater
interoperability with other international statistical systems. The development
of the new DRS platform and its rollout are being coordinated with the
Commonwealth Secretariat (Meridian) and the Debt Management and
Financial Analysis System of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), which
provide the debt management software currently used by about 80 percent of
DRS reporting countries. The goal is a seamless extraction, validation, and
automated pass-through of data recorded by the borrowers in these systems to

the World Bank Group in a format that meets the DRS reporting requirement.
The modernization of the DRS will also expand users’ access to IDS and allow
them to generate customized aggregates and conduct deeper analytical work,
while preserving the strict confidentiality of instrument-level information that
borrowers share with the World Bank Group.
With the new reporting mechanism, DRS reporters will submit data through a
web-based portal that streamlines and facilitates compliance with the World Bank
Group reporting requirements. It provides reporters with an easy-to-use and
efficient method for submitting both data and metadata securely. Reporting is
structured around one reporting template that includes both public and publicly
guaranteed and private nonguaranteed external debt and complementary
modules, which replace the collective of DRS reporting forms previously
used. The new portal enables DRS reporters to download the standardized
reporting template and the related modules, and to upload data and validate
them for consistency before submission to the World Bank Group. To facilitate
reporting, it also includes a hyperlink to the DRS reporting manual and online
how-to guidance for reporters when the reporting validating mechanism flags
inconsistencies in the data being uploaded by the reporter.
Integrating Domestic Public Debt into the Debt Transparency Agenda
A critical new frontier for the debt transparency agenda is the expansion of data
coverage to domestic public debt, which has become an increasingly important
share of LMICs’ public debt. In many of these countries, domestic public debt
now accounts for 40–60 percent of total public debt, and in some of them it
exceeds those shares. Despite the centrality of domestic debt levels to fiscal
sustainability, sound monetary policy, and financial stability, data on domestic
debt obligations remain fragmented, inconsistently defined, and only partially
captured in international data sets. In marked contrast to external public debt,
no comprehensive global platform currently exists to systematically collect and
disseminate detailed, comprehensive, and cross-country comparable domestic
public debt data for LMICs.
The World Bank Group initiative to extend the DRS to domestic public debt
represents a unique contribution to the global data architecture. It is the only
framework currently in development that aims to bring together detailed,
standardized, and cross-country comparable domestic public debt statistics for
LMICs. The integration of domestic and external debt into a single, coherent
reporting system to the DRS opens the door, for the first time, to the creation
of a comprehensive and unified picture of public sector liabilities. This picture
will provide the wherewithal to make a far more accurate assessment of a
93

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
country’s debt sustainability and an evaluation of the fiscal risks domestic debt
obligations pose.
This initiative presents institutional and technical challenges. Extensive diagnostic
work, including surveys and pilot exercises conducted by the World Bank Group
with DRS reporting countries and partner institutions that support them—
including the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, and UNCTAD—identified a
vast and complex array of instruments for raising financing in domestic markets.
In many LMICs, domestic debt is managed by multiple entities, including
ministries of finance, central banks, and subnational governments, and recorded
in different systems using a variety of classifications. An important element
of the new reporting framework will be the introduction of a standardized
reporting template based on international definitions and classifications. It will
be complemented by a detailed reporting manual and comprehensive guidelines
on consolidation of domestic and external public debt across different levels of
government to derive comprehensive and accurate measures of total public sector
liabilities. To support implementation, the World Bank Group is developing
methodological guidance on compiling and reporting domestic debt statistics in
collaboration with the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, UNCTAD, and other
international partners.
Implementation of the domestic debt module represents a major expansion
of the DRS and will require significant institutional reforms and technical
enhancements in many LMICs. These changes include strengthening legal
mandates for data collection, improving coordination across public sector
entities, and upgrading debt management systems. In view of these needs,
the domestic debt reporting framework will be introduced on a phased and
voluntary basis, beginning with central government debt and progressively
expanding to full public sector coverage, thereby allowing LMICs to participate
according to their capacity while simultaneously benefiting from targeted
technical assistance. The World Bank Group is confident that, over time,
full integration of domestic and external debt data into a unified reporting
framework can be achieved with a game-changing impact on debt transparency.
Comprehensive debt statistics will provide critical insights into total public
debt burdens, maturity concentration, interest rate exposure, and rollover risks,
and will enhance the reconciliation of debt records with fiscal and monetary
statistics and overall macroeconomic surveillance.

supported by continuous and structured engagement with participating

Box 3.1 The Indonesia Loan Clearing Module Pilot Project
New standards and protocols for debt data reconciliation supported by innovative
information technology solutions to systematically digitalize and automatically
reconcile public loan data have the potential to ensure better quality recording and
save time and effort. The World Bank Group is already evaluating such standards
and protocols. In 2025, it launched a pilot project in Indonesia, funded by the
Japanese Ministry of Finance, to develop a Loan Clearing Module to facilitate
information sharing between borrowers and official creditors. This module acts as
a platform for information sharing between creditors’ data systems and those of
local debt management offices. For each new transaction (that is, new loan signed,
payment, disbursement, or modification), the originator would create a new data
file electronically transmitted to the platform according to standardized templates.
The counterpart then validates the information and automatically transfers the
data as needed into its own debt recording system. In its first phase, this project
seeks to reconcile loans issued by Indonesia’s largest external lenders (the Japan
International Cooperation Agency, the Asian Development Bank, and the World
Bank Group), before including a wider group of Indonesian official and potential
private sector creditors in the second phase. Implementation of the pilot project
in Indonesia has already demonstrated the technical feasibility of continuous
synchronization and validation of debtor and creditor data. The debt office has
already automatically transferred World Bank Group loan data and uploaded
them into the local debt system; as of May 2026, the platform had successfully
exchanged and validated a total of 761 loan records, and 642 subefforts are under
way to cover other official creditors. Once fully operational, the Loan Clearing
Module codes could be made available to other countries, potentially serving as an
international platform for debt data reconciliation, providing a new, real-time source
of fully validated debt statistics.
Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency
Debt transparency involves much more than encouraging debtors and their
creditors to disclose additional data. Advancing the debt transparency agenda
ultimately depends on strengthening loan records, disbursement records, and
payment records. Producing accurate and comprehensive data to the standard
required for informed fiscal and debt management decision-making requires
strong institutional arrangements, rigorous legal and governance structures,
consistent statistical standards, and robust validation processes.
Building the Foundations of Debt Transparency
Capacity building is an integral part of the World Bank Group’s debt
transparency agenda. Over the past five years, the Debt Statistics Team has

contributed to 23 courses and workshops at the global, regional, and country
levels. These opportunities were complemented by targeted technical assistance
for individual IDA-eligible countries and continuous engagement with other
international organizations and regional banks providing comparable capacity-
building services. Support from the Debt Statistics Team is broad-based and
includes presentations on best practice in monitoring and recording debt data,
advice on how to manage the public debt portfolio and contingent liabilities,
and guidance for understanding and adopting international statistical standards
and definitions. This support is combined with assistance on how to strengthen
institutional systems and human resources responsible for compilation and
dissemination of debt statistics at the national level and to international data
sets. It also builds awareness on how these data factor into decision-making
regarding public borrowing and debt sustainability within the broader framework
of macroeconomic policies. The delivery mechanism has also evolved with a
heightened emphasis on practical training aimed at strengthening the entire
debt data production chain. This training includes all aspects of the data
collection process, from recording individual debt instruments, to institutional
coordination to monitor stocks and flows, data validation and reconciliation, and
dissemination and use of comprehensive debt statistics for analyses and use by
policy makers.
The modernization and expansion of the DRS serves as an important anchor
for structuring the capacity-building program in debt data management. It
currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more
than 50,000 active loan records, with approximately 2,500–3,000 new loans
reported each year. Maintaining a system of this scale and ensuring the integrity
of the data require sustained investment in national reporting capacity. Practical
training sessions are not limited to familiarizing debt managers with the new
and very different DRS reporting structure. They include equally, if not more,
important training in how to implement international statistical standards to
categorize and compile debt data. In this context, the overarching goal is to
also transmit the skills required to determine if data are complete, internally
consistent, appropriately classified, and aligned with international statistical
standards. Workshops provide hands-on experience and test runs of the revised
classifications and reporting requirements, and explain the links between
DRS concepts and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users
(IMF 2014). Such alignments are important because countries should not have
to maintain parallel conceptual frameworks for national external debt statistics
and international reporting. Moreover, consistency between the two reduces the
reporting burden, improves comparability, and enhances the use of DRS data for
the countries’ own debt management and analytical purposes.

The agenda is also expanding beyond external debt. The voluntary rollout
of reporting on domestic public debt creates an opportunity to strengthen
countries’ capacity to produce a more comprehensive picture of total public
sector indebtedness. Over time, this capacity can help reduce the historical divide
between external and domestic debt reporting, and support more integrated
analysis of countries’ overall debt vulnerabilities.
A Partnership-Based Model to Develop Capacity
The World Bank Group’s approach to capacity building to strengthen debt
management is multifaceted and includes regional courses, country-specific
technical assistance, and peer learning delivered in partnerships with other
international organizations. Regional workshops are typically organized as
intensive five-day programs combining technical presentations with exercises,
country cases, simulations, and structured discussions. They allow participants
to apply statistical concepts to the practical problems they encounter in their
daily work. Participation extends beyond debt management offices, and the
World Bank Group strives to bring together, whenever possible, staff from central
banks, ministries of finance, statistical agencies, and other institutions involved
in producing debt information. This cross-institutional approach is important
because weaknesses in debt statistics often arise not from a lack of information
but from fragmentation of that information across multiple government
institutions. Bringing these institutions together can improve understanding
of responsibilities, facilitate data sharing, and strengthen consistency across
national data sets. Partnerships with institutions like the IMF, the Commonwealth
Secretariat, and UNCTAD strengthen the multifaceted approach by contributing
to regional training programs, connecting statistical standards to debt
management practices and reporting requirements, and underscoring the
imperatives of ensuring debt data management systems are updated and validated
on a daily basis. Cooperation with the Commonwealth Secretariat and UNCTAD
is particularly valuable now, as the redesigned DRS is being incorporated into
the debt management systems they have created and maintain in order to embed
methodological changes into national operating environments and to automate
DRS reporting requirements.
Responding to an Increasingly Complex Debt Landscape
Capacity building has also expanded to address areas where weaknesses in
coverage can have significant implications for assessments of public debt and
fiscal risks. One such area is nonguaranteed borrowing by SOEs and other public
sector entities. Identifying these liabilities can be difficult when information is
dispersed across institutions or when debt management systems focus primarily
on central government borrowing. Training therefore helps participants identify
98

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
institutional coverage gaps and understand how nonguaranteed and contingent
liabilities should be captured and classified. More attention is also being given to
emerging and complex instruments. As sovereign financing evolves and lending
instruments become more complex, methodological guidance on how to account
for them and expertise in assessing the risks they may pose takes on added
importance.
An important evolution in the capacity-building program has been its integration
into the World Bank Group’s mainstream work on data quality and debt
sustainability. Data discrepancies are increasingly being seen not simply as errors
to be corrected but as diagnostic information that offers insights into weaknesses
in national systems. The annual reconciliation of debtor and creditor information
is a good example. Differences may reveal problems in creditor classification,
exchange rate conversion, recording of arrears, treatment of restructurings,
institutional coverage, or the timing of transactions. Working through these
discrepancies directly with country authorities provides an opportunity to identify
their causes and improve compilation practices at the source. The same principle
underpins the work of harmonizing the data to the DRS and the data national
authorities provide for the debt sustainability analyses conducted jointly by the
IMF and the World Bank Group. Improvements in the timeliness and quality of
reporting to the DRS by IDA-eligible countries offer clear indications that these
measures are having a positive knock-on effect.
Providing Continuous and Scalable Learning
Traditional face-to-face training is valuable and essential, particularly
where participants need to work through country-specific institutional and
methodological issues. But the scale of training required, coupled with the
turnover of staff in national debt offices, is such that capacity building cannot
be delivered exclusively through periodic workshops. The next phase is therefore
moving toward a more continuous model combining regional training, targeted
technical assistance, methodological guidance, and digital learning. Training
materials are being developed in conjunction with the updated DRS Manual and
reporting guidance, and collaboration with the World Bank Group Data Academy
can provide structured e-learning modules that countries can access between
formal training events.
This approach can create a more sustainable capacity-building ecosystem with
introductory modules providing a common foundation for new debt compilers
and specialized modules to address topics such as restructuring, arrears,
contingent liabilities, creditor classification, domestic debt, and new financial
instruments. Online tools such as validation guides and step-by-step guides to
reporting templates, test exercises, and case studies can support participants
99

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
after formal training has ended. This support will enable regional or country
workshops to focus on practical applications and more complex cases and create
the space for peer learning, which will remain an important part of this model.
Countries frequently face similar challenges, and regional workshops provide an
opportunity to exchange practical solutions and institutional experiences that
cannot easily be captured in manuals. Group exercises and simulations have
demonstrated the value of allowing participants to work jointly through real
reporting and classification problems.
From Capacity Building to Sustainable Debt Transparency
Success is not measured by the number of people trained but by the improvement
in the coverage, quality, and transparency of the debt data countries produce.
It requires institutional and instrument coverage, more timely submissions,
fewer unexplained discrepancies, better reconciliation between national and
international data sets, and greater public availability of debt information,
and can be achieved only by tailoring and adapting capacity-building activities
to country circumstances and needs. For some countries, the primary need is
methodological training; for others, it centers on institutional improvements
in debt management systems, assistance in reconciling databases, or extending
coverage of public sector debt to SOEs, contingent liabilities, or domestic debt.
Diagnostic information from DRS reporting, data validation, debtor-creditor
reconciliation, and comparisons with other international data sets are increasingly
being used to target technical assistance to areas where they will have the greatest
impact. The World Bank Group’s role extends beyond collecting debt data, to
supporting LMICs to build the human capital and institutional arrangements
and the systems required to produce them. Sustainable improvements in debt
transparency depend on strong national institutions with the capacity to generate
reliable information.
As both external and domestic financing for LMICs becomes more complex, this
investment will become even more important. New creditors, new instruments,
growing domestic debt markets, and greater attention to public sector and
contingent liabilities are expanding the information countries need to manage
them. Capacity building must evolve alongside these developments if borrowers
are to keep pace. Ultimately, more reliable debt data and stronger national
capacity go hand in hand and reinforce each other. More robust institutions
produce better statistics, which in turn underscore inherent weaknesses and
permit technical support to be targeted more effectively; and stronger national
systems make improvements in debt transparency more durable. Capacity
building is not complementary to the debt transparency agenda; rather, it is one of
the foundations on which the agenda stands.
100

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
Debt Asymmetries
Transparent external and public debt data are fundamental to assessing LMICs’
financial situations. These data provide the foundation for debt sustainability
analysis, managing fiscal and monetary policy, and disclosure of the level and
composition of existing obligations to creditors, investors, development partners,
and citizens. The expectation is that debt transparency will bring clarity with a
definitive account of a country’s debt situation. All too often, however, the debt
data disseminated by LMICs differ from creditors’ claims, raising doubts about
data accuracy, under-recording, or, worse, deliberate nondisclosure and hidden
debt. Although these situations are sometimes the case, the primary challenge
to the accuracy, credibility, and comparability of debt data is asymmetries,
particularly between debtor- and creditor-reported figures.
Addressing Debt Asymmetries Is Key to Debt Transparency
Asymmetries in debt data arise primarily from inconsistent methodological
definitions and accounting practices in debtor and creditor countries and other
institutions that compile and disseminate debt data. These divergent practices
present a minefield for users trying to compare debtor and creditor data or to
make cross-country comparisons across groups of debtors or creditors. In extreme
cases discrepancies as large as 30 percent of gross domestic product have been
observed in debt stock figures purporting to have the same coverage. Issues as
simple as classification of domestic and external debt on a currency basis will
likely result in a very different number for external debt stocks than the one
disseminated by the World Bank Group in IDS, which uses the international
standard residency criterion. Conversely, IDS may legitimately record a lower
figure for external debt owed to a creditor than the creditor itself records. This
discrepancy occurs because the IDS figure excludes loans to nonguaranteed
private sector borrowers, not separately identifiable in the aggregate data reported
to the DRS. Mitigating data asymmetries is key to being able to validate debt data
and confirm those data to be comprehensive and accurate, a core objective of the
debt transparency agenda.
The Reasons for Asymmetries in Debt Data
One of the key reasons for debt data asymmetries is the existence of multiple
data sources. The primary sources are debtor and creditor accounting, and data
collection frameworks. The main actors in debtor countries are debt management
offices, finance ministries, central banks, and national statistical agencies,
which have varying institutional mandates and data collection mechanisms.
In creditor countries, there are the databases of bilateral lending agencies
101

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
such as aid ministries, official export credit agencies, and public sector banks.
International financial institutions like the IMF and the World Bank Group are
important creditors, and they play a central role in the compilation of global debt
and other external sector statistics. Similarly, the Organisation for Economic
Co-operation and Development (OECD) collects and disseminates data on aid
flows and bilateral loans, and the Bank for International Settlements does the
same for financing by the banking sector. There are also databases that capture
information on market-based sources of financing collated by private companies
such as Dealogic. Annex 3A provides a summary of the focus and coverage of the
key debt databases.
Asymmetries in debt data also stem from a whole range of factors, including
differences in coverage, timing of recording, institutional practice, and delayed
reporting by borrowers and creditors. Coverage often differs—debtor-based
systems may exclude private nonguaranteed borrowing, whereas creditor-side
data likely capture these flows more comprehensively. Recording practices
vary: some compilers adopt accrual-based accounting (recognizing transactions
when obligations arise), whereas others use the cash basis method (recording
payments when they are made). These divergent practices lead to timing and
value mismatches. Another common source of asymmetry is valuation, which
uses different exchange rates or accounting methods. For example, compilations
based on the face value versus the market value for bond issues will result
in very different figures for outstanding balances. Divergent valuation rules
for inflation-indexed or floating-rate instruments can further widen the gap
between data sets.
Numerous inconsistencies also occur in instrument classification and
sectorization—that is, how borrowers are classified and captured in public or
private sector debt data. Methodological discrepancies are frequently embedded
in national statistical practices and international reporting frameworks, creating
challenges for users trying to reconcile external and public debt data across
sources. Trade credits and advances may be included in external debt statistics in
some countries and unaccounted for in others. Loans extended by state-owned
banks may be classified as public debt on the creditor side but recorded as private
debt by the debtor. Differences in the classification of borrowers, particularly
SOEs, central banks, and government-guaranteed entities, can lead to significant
discrepancies between data sets. Some statistical systems treat SOEs as part of the
public sector, whereas others classify them as private unless explicitly guaranteed.
Similarly, contingent liabilities and guarantees may be included in debt totals
in some frameworks but excluded until they are triggered in others, producing
further divergence in reported figures.
102

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
International institutions have stepped up efforts to harmonize the compilation
of debt statistics. The IMF and the Task Force on Finance Statistics promote
the use of standardized statistical frameworks such as External Debt Statistics:
Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014) and are currently supporting updates
to better account for evolving borrowing trends, including state-contingent debt
instruments and collateralized borrowing. The Quarterly External Debt Statistics
platform, comanaged by the IMF and the World Bank Group, enables countries
to submit quarterly data aligned with international standards, thereby improving
consistency and transparency. Other important initiatives include the World
Bank Group Debt Transparency Initiatives and the IDA Sustainable Development
Finance Policy, both of which tie financial support to improvements in debt
reporting.
As already discussed, the core objective of the major revamp of the World Bank
Group DRS is harmonization of reporting standards and definitions for LMICs
with agreed international methodology, including the IMF’s Integrated Balance
of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (IMF 2025) and the
United Nations Statistics Division’s 2025 System of National Accounts, supported
by dedicated capacity building. Many asymmetries could also be avoided through
automation and system integration. Developing centralized platforms that link
balance of payments, international investment position statistics, and external
debt data, and enable interoperability between debt management systems and
other external sector statistics databases, would force consistency and minimize
manual errors. Emerging technologies such as discrepancy detectors powered by
artificial intelligence or SDMX-based data exchanges would further modernize
data compilation workflows.
From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge
For more than seven decades, the World Bank Group DRS has transformed
detailed information reported by borrowing countries into one of the world’s
most comprehensive sources of internationally comparable external debt
statistics. It provides a statistical infrastructure for understanding not simply how
much countries owe but who borrowed from whom, through which instruments,
and on what terms, and how those obligations evolve over time.
At its core, the program is a continuous data-to-knowledge process. Detailed
information reported by borrowing countries is systematically validated,
reconciled, and standardized before being transformed into internationally
comparable debt statistics. These statistics are then analyzed and placed in their
broader economic and financial context, turning granular country reporting
103

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
into evidence that can inform debt management, debt sustainability assessments,
financing decisions, and the global policy debate.
The World Bank Group debt transparency work is built as a continuous chain
of value through three-tier architecture (refer to annex 3B for more information
on the World Bank Group Debt Statistics three-tier architecture): DRS provides
the granular evidence, IDS transforms that evidence into trusted and transparent
statistical facts, and the International Debt Report (IDR) converts those facts into
analysis and actionable knowledge. Together, these three tiers connect country-
level debt reporting to the broader development and policy agenda.
A loan reported by a national debt office can serve as a globally comparable
indicator, reveal a change in creditor or financing patterns, expose an information
gap or emerging vulnerability, inform a debt sustainability assessment or
restructuring discussion, and contribute to international policy discussions on
sustainable finance and debt transparency.
This process also works in reverse. Transparency gaps, new financing instruments,
emerging vulnerabilities, and methodological challenges identified through IDS
and IDR analysis feed directly back into the DRS. They inform improvements in
reporting requirements, classifications, validation rules, reconciliation procedures,
methodological guidance, and engagement with both borrowers and creditors.
Debt transparency is therefore not a one-time disclosure exercise but a continuous
cycle of reporting, validation, reconciliation, dissemination, analysis, and
improvement.
This architecture is also central to the World Bank Group’s broader debt
transparency agenda. Greater transparency about the amount, composition,
terms, and creditors of public debt is essential for sound debt management,
credible debt sustainability assessments, effective restructuring, and informed
lending and investment decisions. By strengthening reporting standards,
improving data quality, reconciling debtor and creditor records, expanding
the information available to users, and identifying remaining data gaps, the
DRS provides the statistical foundation on which greater debt transparency
can be built.
This approach also reflects an important evolution in the international debt
transparency agenda: responsibility does not rest solely with borrowing countries.
Comprehensive debt transparency requires coordinated action by borrowers,
bilateral and multilateral creditors, private lenders, international financial
institutions, and other stakeholders. The World Bank Group’s role is increasingly
to connect these actors around common definitions, stronger reporting practices,
better reconciliation, and more accessible and reliable debt information.
104

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
The result is more than a debt database. It is a global statistical infrastructure
for debt transparency that connects individual debt obligations to a broader
understanding of financing flows, creditor relationships, fiscal pressures, and
debt sustainability, while helping make sovereign borrowing increasingly visible,
comparable, credible, and accountable.
Ultimately, strengthening debt transparency comes down to ensuring that public
borrowing remains a tool for development rather than a source of vulnerability.
By improving the availability and reliability of debt data, countries are better
equipped to manage risks, design effective policies, and engage transparently
with stakeholders. For creditors and markets, enhanced transparency supports
more accurate risk assessment and more efficient allocation of capital. For the
international community, it contributes to a more stable and resilient global
financial system. Sustained investment in this agenda is not only advisable, but it
is also necessary for positive long-term development outcomes.
Annex 3A. Sources of Debt Statistics
Debt statistics originate from a diverse set of sources, classified broadly into
debtor-based and creditor-based data sets. Each has unique strengths as well as
limitations that may lead to discrepancies.
Debtor-Based Sources
Debtor-based data are sourced from countries that borrow, typically through
institutions such as finance ministries, debt management offices, or central
banks. These data are reported to international sources like the World Bank
Group’s DRS and the IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment
Position. Although rich in detail, debtor-based data sources reflect the borrower’s
operational realities and often omit or underreport certain types of debt, such as
short-term borrowing and borrowing in the form of debt securities and private
sector liabilities, or debt from SOEs without sovereign guarantees.
The DRS covers long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, along
with aggregate information for private nonguaranteed debt when available.
Data are reported on an instrument-by-instrument basis, providing detailed
information on terms, disbursements, debt service, and outstanding amounts.
The key strength of the DRS is the depth and consistency of coverage for LMICs,
enabling granular analysis. Its main limitation is the absence of short-term debt
and certain debt instruments, such as pension fund liabilities (owed to national
households but held by nonresidents), currency and deposits, and trade credit and
advances. Moreover, the aggregation of private nonguaranteed debt reporting
105

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
may mask incomplete coverage and can obscure the characteristics of specific
instruments.
The IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position
frameworks capture external debt as part of the broader international accounts,
including components such as direct investment debt, portfolio debt, and other
investment debt (for example, loans and trade credit and advances). The key
strength of these data is their alignment with global macroeconomic accounts,
ensuring comparability across countries. The principal limitation is that
they are published in aggregate form, masking important details such as the
instrument type, currency composition, interest rate structure, maturity profile,
creditor sector, and other specifics like collateralization, governing law, and
repayment schedules. It warrants mention that the use of original maturity in the
International Investment Position, and thus the unavailability of statistics on a
remaining maturity basis, significantly limits the use of International Investment
Position external debt–related statistics for debt sustainability analysis.
National debt management systems such as the Commonwealth Secretariat’s
Meridian, UNCTAD’s Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, and
country-specific custom-built platforms are used by borrowers to record, monitor,
and manage public debt, often serving as the source of data submitted to the
World Bank Group or IMF. Their strength lies in the operational detail they
capture to support day-to-day debt management decisions. Their limitation lies in
inconsistency in how these systems are used and the accuracy and completeness of
the data recorded in them. These strengths and limitations vary significantly and
largely mirror a country’s institutional and technical capacity.
Creditor-Based Sources
The creditor-based sources reflect the viewpoint of the lending institutions, such
as donor governments, commercial banks, and bondholders. These sources
include the OECD’s Creditor Reporting System, the Bank for International
Settlements statistics, and data collated by the Paris Club. Although these sources
often provide visibility into bilateral and private sector lending, their coverage
may be limited geographically or in terms of the types of instruments covered.
Discrepancies between these sources are at the heart of many data asymmetries.
These sources reflect the view of those who provide financing, often more
complete for bilateral and private sector debt.
The OECD Creditor Reporting System tracks official bilateral loans and grants
from members of the Development Assistance Committee and from export credit
agencies. It contains detailed information on aspects such as concessionality,
maturity, and the intended purpose of financing. Its key strength is its dedicated
106

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
focus on development finance, providing detailed insights into aid flows and
related terms. Its main limitation is its restricted coverage to official and officially
supported lending by OECD member countries.
The Bank for International Settlements compiles data from commercial banks
on cross-border claims and liabilities through two primary data sets: Locational
Banking Statistics, which reports according to the location of the reporting
bank; and Consolidated Banking Statistics, which reports banks’ global claims
on other countries. Its strength lies in providing timely data on private financial
flows, particularly from the banking sector, making it valuable for near-real-time
monitoring of cross-border lending trends. Its limitation is that the data are not at
the loan level and may not align with debtor country classifications, reducing its
utility for detailed debt instrument analysis or reconciliation with national statistics.
The Paris Club, private sector data collection entities like Dealogic, and some
export credit agencies supply information on bilateral debt restructurings,
syndicated loans and international bond issues, and direct and guaranteed export
credits. Their strength is that they offer unique insights into certain types of
financing—such as officially supported export credits and market-based lending—
that are often underrepresented in other data sets. Their limitation is that the
information is fragmented, not systematically compiled, and often not publicly
available in a timely manner, creating gaps in comprehensive debt monitoring.
Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier
Architecture
The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Program operates through a three-
tier architecture that progressively transforms granular country reporting into
internationally comparable statistics and policy-relevant knowledge, while
strengthening transparency at every stage of the process (figure 3B.1).
Tier 1: DRS—The Granular Data Foundation
Established in 1951, the DRS is one of the world’s longest-running sovereign
debt reporting systems. Today, it covers roughly 120 low- and middle-income
reporting economies and provides a uniquely detailed historical record extending
over more than 70 years. IBRD and IDA borrowers report detailed information
on their long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, including
new commitments, outstanding stocks, and annual transactions. Private
nonguaranteed external debt is also incorporated in aggregate form. At this first
tier, the data answer four fundamental questions: Who borrowed? From whom?
On what terms? And what happened to the debt over time? These questions are

The DRS provides the granular data infrastructure needed to identify,
measure, and track debt exposures over time. At the individual debt level, it
captures detailed information on borrowers, creditors, instruments, currencies,
commitments, disbursements, debt service, arrears, and restructurings,
providing insight not only into the amount of debt outstanding but also into its
composition, financing terms, repayment profile, and evolution. As sovereign
financing instruments and practices continue to evolve, DRS reporting
requirements, classifications, and methodological guidance are continuously
strengthened to ensure that this growing complexity is reflected in comprehensive,
consistent, and increasingly complete coverage of countries’ debt obligations and
financing arrangements.
Tier 2: IDS—From Granular Records to Trusted and Transparent Statistics
Debt transparency depends not only on the availability of information but also
on its quality, consistency, comparability, and credibility. Individual debt records
become meaningful global statistics only after they have been standardized and
made comparable across countries and over time. This transformation takes
place through the production of the IDS database. The second tier moves beyond
108

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy
individual transactions to answer the following questions: What happened?
Where did it happen? How are financing patterns changing? How do countries
compare? And where do important information gaps remain?
The statistical production process involves the compilation of the external debt
statistics using standardized methodologies, definitions, and classifications. This
process is critical to ensure that published statistics accurately reflect countries’
debt. IDS adds value across four critical dimensions: (a) comparability, through
common concepts and classifications across economies; (b) consistency, through
reconciliation of stocks, flows, transactions, and revisions; (c) historical series,
which make it possible to identify structural changes in global financing; and
(d) accessibility, through public databases, downloadable data sets, country and
regional tables, and analytical products.
Tier 3: IDR—From Trusted Statistics to Actionable Knowledge
The annual IDR represents the analytical tier of architecture. It combines the
depth of the underlying DRS information and the consistency of IDS statistics
with economic and policy analysis.
Where the DRS captures what countries report, and IDS establishes what
happened, the IDR examines why it happened, why it matters, who is most
exposed and more vulnerable, and what policy makers should watch next. For
more than five decades, the World Bank Group’s annual debt publication has
documented major transformations in international development finance, from
the debt crises of the 1980s and the emergence of global bond markets, to debt-
relief initiatives, the rise of new bilateral and private creditors, increasingly
complex financing instruments, and today’s environment of elevated borrowing
costs and debt service pressures. The IDR places these developments in their
wider economic context. It serves as both an analytical publication and an
important instrument of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency agenda by
highlighting where improvements in reporting, disclosure, creditor information,
and debt management practices are most needed.

APPENDIX

Data Sources
The principal source of information for the tables in International Debt Report
2026 is the International Debt Statistics database, which is based on reports to
the World Bank through the World Bank’s Debtor Reporting System (DRS) from
member countries that have received either International Bank for Reconstruction
and Development loans or International Development Association credits. The
DRS has its origin in the World Bank’s need to monitor and assess the financial
position of its borrowers. Since 1951, borrowers have been required to provide
statistics on their public external debt and private sector debt that benefit from
a public guarantee. Reporting countries submit reports on the annual status,
transactions, and terms of the long-term external debt of public agencies and that
of private ones guaranteed by a public agency in the debtor country. The DRS
maintains these records on a loan-by-loan basis. In 1973, coverage of the DRS
was expanded to include private sector nonguaranteed borrowing; however, for
this category of debt, data are provided by borrowers in aggregate rather than
loan by loan.
Data submitted to the DRS are processed in the World Bank External Debt
system, along with additional information received from the African Development
Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and
Development, the Inter-American Development Bank, the International Monetary
Fund, and institutions of the World Bank Group (International Bank for
Reconstruction and Development and International Development Association).
The World Bank External Debt is an internal system of the World Bank. Among
its outputs is the International Debt Statistics database, from which the tables and
data visualizations in this publication and the online database are produced.
Data on exports and imports (on a balance of payments basis), international
reserves, current account balances, foreign direct investment on equity, portfolio
equity flows, and primary income on foreign direct investment are drawn
mainly from the International Monetary Fund, supplemented by UN Trade and
Development reports and country data. Balance of payments data are presented
according to the sixth edition of the International Monetary Fund’s Balance of
Payments Manual. Official aid flows come from data collected and published
by the Development Assistance Committee of the Organisation for Economic
Co-operation and Development. Short-term external debt data are as reported by
debtor countries or are estimates based on the Bank for International Settlements
243

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026
quarterly series of commercial banks’ claims on low- and middle-income
countries. For some countries, estimates were prepared by pooling creditor and
debtor information. Data on the gross national income of most low- and middle-
income countries are collected from national statistical organizations or central
banks by visiting and resident World Bank missions.
Every effort has been made to ensure the accuracy and completeness of the
external debt statistics. Coverage has been improved through the efforts of the
reporting agencies and close collaboration between the World Bank and its
partners, the Commonwealth Secretariat and UN Trade and Development, which
provide debt recording and reporting systems across the globe, as well as through
the work of the World Bank missions, which visit member countries to gather
data and to provide technical assistance on debt issues. Nevertheless, quality and
coverage vary among debtors and may also vary for the same debtor from year to
year. Data on long-term external debt reported by member countries are checked
against, and supplemented by, data from several other sources. Among these
sources are the statements and reports of several regional development banks,
government lending agencies, and official government websites.

Glossary
This list provides general descriptions, not precise legal definitions, of the terms
commonly used in this report. However, the descriptions include legal and policy
elements relevant to how these terms are understood and applied in practice.
Base year is the period against which quantities and prices of a given period are
compared.
Bilateral currency swap line is an agreement between two central banks to
exchange a cash flow in one currency against a cash flow in another currency
according to predetermined terms and conditions.
Blue bond is a debt instrument issued by governments, development banks, or
other entities to raise capital from impact investors to finance marine and ocean-
based projects that yield positive environmental, economic, and climate benefits.
Bonds are debt instruments issued by public and publicly guaranteed or private
debtors with durations of one year or longer. Bonds usually give the holder
the unconditional right to fixed money income or to contractually determined,
variable money income.
Central bank is a country’s financial institution that exercises control over key
aspects of the financial system. It carries out activities such as issuing currency,
managing international reserves, transacting with the International Monetary
Fund, and providing credit to deposit-taking corporations.
Commitments (of public and publicly guaranteed debt) constitute the total
amount of new long-term loans to public sector borrowers or to borrowers with
a public sector guarantee extended by official and private lenders and for which
contracts were signed in the year specified.
Common Framework for debt treatment beyond the Debt Service Suspension
Initiative is an initiative launched in 2022 and endorsed by the Group of
Twenty, designed to support, in a structural manner, low-income countries with
unsustainable debt.
Concessional debt conveys information about the borrower’s receipt of aid from
official lenders at concessional terms as defined by the World Bank, that is, loans
with an original grant element of 35 percent or more. The World Bank classifies

loans from major regional development banks—the African Development Bank,
Asian Development Bank, and Inter-American Development Bank—as
concessional.
Debt buyback is the repurchase by a debtor of its own debt, either at a discount
price or at par value. In the event of a buyback of long-term debt, the face value
of the debt bought back will be recorded as a decline in stock outstanding of
long-term debt, and the cash amount received by creditors will be recorded as a
principal repayment.
Debt distress, as defined under the International Monetary Fund–World Bank
Debt Sustainability Framework (DSF) for low-income countries, is caused by
unsustainable debt, wherein a country is unable to fulfill its financial obligations
and debt restructuring is required.
Debt-distressed is when a country’s debt and debt service ratios significantly
and persistently breach established thresholds, indicating an inability to meet
the country’s financial obligations. It is the most severe risk category in the
International Monetary Fund–World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework (DSF)
for low-income countries.
Debt-for-climate swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments
related to climate activities.
Debt-for-development swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments
related to a specific development goal, such as nature conservation, climate
action, education, nutrition, or support for refugees.
Debt-for-equity swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments
related to equity investments.
Debt-for-nature swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments
related to conservation activities.
Debt restructurings are revisions to debt service obligations agreed on by creditors
and debtors. Such agreements change the amount and timing of future principal
and interest payments. Debt restructuring is a complex process that requires the
agreement of domestic and foreign creditors and involves burden sharing between
different parties (for example, between residents and banks in most restructurings
of domestic debt).
Debt service is the sum of principal repayments and interest paid on total long-
term debt (public and publicly guaranteed debt and private nonguaranteed debt).
Debt Service Suspension Initiative (DSSI) took effect on May 1, 2020, and
allowed 73 eligible countries to apply for a temporary suspension of debt service
